title: Vampire Planet: The Case for Letting Malibu Flood
author: Joshua Frank
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_1261-680x510.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/11/vampire-
planet-the-case-for-letting-malibu-flood/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_1262-680x510.jpeg)

A coastline erodes as sea levels rise. Long Beach, California. Photo by Joshua
Frank.

**This week in the Anthropocene**

The first major swell of the year pummeled Southern California this week, and
onlookers flocked to ritzy Balboa Peninsula in Newport Beach to watch
adrenaline junkies attack the Wedge – a mutant wave that ricochets off a rock
jetty, forming a steep, heavy [wall of
water](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZXp_a3z5tR/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==)
that accelerates and breaks chaotically. Only the bravest (craziest?) dare to
face it down.

A wild storm system, [nearly the
size](https://www.instagram.com/p/DZSmZC4hcxy/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=embed_video_watch_again)
of the United States, took shape in the central South Pacific last week and
hurled massive wave energy toward California and Baja, Mexico. It was the
perfect setup to awaken the sleeping Wedge and the lore and danger that
accompany the [deadly](https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2009-jul-25-me-
beaches25-story.html) break. As the big swell arrived on Tuesday, lifeguards
were already [rescuing](https://www.ocregister.com/2026/06/09/massive-surf-
hits-the-coast-and-brings-beach-hazards-mutant-wedge-draws-crowds/) daredevils
from the rough waters.

However, amid all the excitement, _er_ , stoke, as we surfers call it, lies a
coastline that continues to be chewed up by high tides, large swells, and
rising seas. The Wedge, for example, is slowly encroaching on multimillion-
dollar beachfront property, forcing the City of Newport to bulldoze mounds of
sand onto the beach in hopes of fending off erosion. It’s a relentless problem
that is set to worsen in the years ahead as climate breakdown continues.

Of course, it’s not only this stretch of the Orange County coast that’s in
danger of having its beaches swallowed by the ocean. In Long Beach, where I
live, sand is continually brought in to protect pricey homes along the city’s
peninsula from flooding as the ocean expands as the icebergs melt. It’s a
[conundrum](https://fox5sandiego.com/news/local-news/coastal/ap-powerful-
pacific-swell-brings-threat-of-more-dangerous-surf-to-
california/?utm_medium=referral&utm_source=facebook.com&utm_campaign=socialflow&fbclid=IwY2xjawSVdFlleHRuA2FlbQIxMQBicmlkETJUYTUzVkdzdThNZlo4MVNYc3J0YwZhcHBfaWQQMjIyMDM5MTc4ODIwMDg5MgABHi6XgkWtDemdBVWpmflvps5QlzdLgAMS4212onj0LZZQjHlQc9PmHSsabTtj_aem_aEW8NRM0CBsygPXr5bwpAQ)
plaguing much of California. [![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/Screen-
Shot-2026-05-20-at-1.49.09-PM.png)](https://www.pilsencommunitybooks.com/item/UfU8gx4LO98oZP-
hvrl3zQ)

Malibu, Dana Point, San Francisco, Seal Beach, and many other coastal cities
are experiencing severe erosion, prompting them to adopt novel approaches,
often trucking in sand as a stopgap to protect property. Taxpayers usually
foot the bill to protect some of the country's most expensive real estate from
the wrath of climate change.

The California Coastal Commission has been sounding the alarm, but few are
listening.

The agency that regulates coastal development
[reports](https://www.coastal.ca.gov/climate/slr/) that sea-level rise in the
state “will affect almost every facet of our natural and built environments.”
If greenhouse gas emissions continue at their current pace, we could see [sea
levels rise](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-
climate/climate-change-global-sea-level) by up to 8 inches over the next
eighty years, or, under the worst-case scenario, by up to 7 feet by 2100 and
13 feet by 2150. NOAA [notes](https://www.climate.gov/news-
features/understanding-climate/climate-change-global-sea-level) that high-tide
flooding is now nearly 900% more frequent than it was just 50 years ago.

Much of this depends on the rate of ice shelf melting - and melting it is. As
Robert Hunziker recently
[wrote](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/05/22/global-warming-icon-doomsday-
glacier-in-trouble/) in CounterPunch, the “Doomsday Glacier” in Antarctica is
acting up.

That’s [very, very bad news](https://thwaitesglacier.org/), not just for
California's 840-mile coast, but for the entire world.

In the best-case scenario, California will still be violently whalloped in the
years to come. In the worst-case scenario, two-thirds of Southern California's
beaches could be [lost](https://www.ppic.org/publication/sea-level-rise-in-
california/) by 2100 unless there is significant, rapid intervention. The
situation isn’t much better up north. The Public Policy Institute of
California [explains](https://www.ppic.org/publication/sea-level-rise-in-
california/) that what's unfolded in the San Francisco Bay illustrates the
peril we’re in. The Bay Area faces a $105 billion shortfall to fortify its
vulnerable coastline.

In Los Angeles, it will cost [$6.4 billion](https://www.wired.com/story/los-
angeles-sea-level-rise/) to adapt, [$246
million](https://lbpost.com/news/study-finds-long-beach-would-have-to-
spend-246-million-in-the-next-20-years-to-hold-back-rising-sea-levels/) in
Long Beach, and up to [$1
billion](https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2019/06/20/paying-the-toll-on-
sea-level-rise/) in San Diego. The only reasonable option is to relocate homes
away from the coast, but the rich aren't ready to budge.

This, as you are likely aware, is among the most expensive real estate in the
world. Homes in Malibu [average](https://www.foxla.com/news/america-most-
expensive-zip-codes-california) $5.9 million. Homes in Newport Beach? An
[average](https://www.foxla.com/news/america-most-expensive-zip-codes-
california) of $9 million. The closer you are to the water, the higher the
price and the greater the risk that someday your lavish pad will be flooded by
rising seas.

There'll be no escaping climate chaos. Warmer oceans also mean stronger, more
intense storm systems, like the one that brought huge waves to So Cal this
week. Larger swells mean greater damage to this embattled coast. Combine all
of this with increasing sea levels, and it’s a recipe for disaster.

Back in Long Beach, I grab lunch and head to the beach. As I unwrap my
burrito, I watch large dump trucks pile up a hill of sand while a tractor
moves and spreads it down the peninsula. Waves don’t batter this beach like
they do at the Wedge down in Newport because a breakwater a mile and a half
out blocks wave action here. Even with the seawall, a lack of natural sand
movement and rising sea levels have made the area vulnerable to frequent
flooding. When (not if) the next 100-year flood hits this stretch of coast, at
least 1,900 homes in Long Beach, worth over [$1.3
billion](https://lbpost.com/news/climate-change/sea-level-rise-naples-
peninsula-belmont-shore/), will be impacted. Many will be destroyed.

There may be no stopping the ocean from warming and the seas from rising, and
I am not in the camp that believes taxpayers should continue paying to protect
these elite coastal properties while people remain unhoused and rents
skyrocket. One day, the effort to protect these homes won’t be enough, and the
water will win.

Mike Davis [argued](https://www.jstor.org/stable/3984830) that we should let
Malibu burn. Well, we should probably let the place flood, too.

+++

The UN released a report predicting that the
[rate](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/jun/08/un-world-ocean-
assessment-severe-stress-sea-level-rise-doubles-pollution-fishing-climate) of
sea level rise will double over the next decade. The Trump administration
isn’t worried and is ensuring that future revelations like this never see the
light of day. The lunatics in Washington have dismantled the National Science
Foundation’s $368 million deep-ocean observation system that tracks many
things, including how the climate is impacting our oceans. This, as the
government spends [$12.6 billion](https://migflug.com/jetflights/28000-cheap-
cruise-missiles-from-cargo-planes/) on a new fleet of cruise missiles. We are
a country in rapid decline.

Want to see the future our coasts face? Check out NOAA’s visualization tool
([click launch](https://coast.noaa.gov/digitalcoast/tools/slr.html)) before
it’s gone.

Lastly, summer is here, and most of the United States is [facing deadly
heatwaves](https://www.redcross.org/about-us/news-and-events/news/2026/deadly-
heat-spreading-across-most-of-us.html) this week. We’ve been [smashing
temperature records](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/extreme-u-s-
heat-wave-smashes-all-time-hottest-march-temperature-record/) all year, and
this summer is sure to be the hottest ever. Miranda Green
[reports](https://atmos.earth/political-landscapes/the-winters-snow-drought-
is-now-a-full-blown-water-crisis/) in _Atmos_ that we are in the early stages
of a full-blown crisis as drought and heat engulf the West.

+++

Okay, as always, a bit of [good news](https://grist.org/solutions/for-first-
time-americans-are-getting-more-of-their-electricity-from-solar-than-coal/).
For the first time ever, Americans are now getting more of their energy from
solar power than from coal. I like the sound of that, well, until I realize
lots of that energy came at a cost as well, to places we ought to be fighting
to protect, [like the Mojave](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/05/vampire-
planet-data-centers-are-worse-than-you-think/).

Light that up, and I’ll see you in a couple of weeks when I return from
Montana.
